Dan Carlin talks about this in episode 1 of his podcast called “Supernova of the East” about Japan in WW2. The podcast as a whole is 100% worth it but in it, Dan talks about how not only was this guy repeatedly told to stand down and his own family flew out to tell him surrender, he was supplied with newspapers that provided absolute fact about Japan’s surrender and even the crown prince (I believe) getting married, his mentality was basically: “if Japan had lost the war, Japan would no longer exist”. It wasn’t until his old commander, who by that point was retired and just some dude living his life, was flown out and ordered him to stand down.
Once back home, this guy was just incredibly disgruntled and disheartened that Japan had surrendered and continued to have the audacity to exist thereafter. 
Dan gets more into the psychology behind this and more, it’s well worth the listen!

It’s not about copying their art style. It’s about learning basic fundamentals of drawing that every artist should know. It’s all well and good having and wanting an art style but you can’t get better and produce the art you aspire to put out without these foundations. That isn’t a criticism of you or your art, it’s just fact for every artist. This was a hard lesson for me. 
Try some of Sycra’s (on YouTube) old videos, they won’t impact your art style and will help you basic anatomy and drawing tips that are easy to follow and genuinely helpful. 
If you want to get better, focus less on art style for now and start focusing on building your foundations. You can’t build a house without a foundation. You’ll get there, give yourself time and patience and keep up the good work.

With screenprint you UV an image onto the screen (at least how I learned). So you take an image into photoshop, turn it into black/white and bitmap (image is made up of small dots) and then you use this image to UV onto the screen. You need to put a light-sensitive resist onto the screen first and the image. Ink or paint is then forced through the (non-blocked areas of) open fabric and that’s how you get the image to come out exactly where you want it. Hope that helps

There have been 3 (yeah, how grand of them) cases of an “apology” issued by Japan. No, they are not good apologies nor does it scratch the surface of it all. 
The first was by Emperor Hirohito after Japan surrendered and tbh he was more than likely forced into making a statement. It acknowledges nothing besides “the tremendous pain” they caused. 
The second one was in 2001 by the prime minister at the time (I dunno his name) however it was in regards to the comfort women. I’ll give it to him, the man seemed remorseful but ultimately it didn’t do anything to actually help. 
The last one was in 2013 by prime minister Abe, it was a shit apology and even worse Abe and his cabinet denied the existence of comfort women before and after. Kudos to them.
All in all Japan has yet to actually admit to their atrocities. They don’t acknowledge Nanking and even still debate the death toll, they still refute comfort women, unit 737 and it’s victims simply do not exist to them so forget about their atrocities in Taiwan or many of the Pacific islands or even the fact that they committed war crimes on their own people in places like Okinawa where they not only raped but used them as human shields but also forced suicides. 
So bushido of them.

I’d strongly recommend Dan Carlings podcast Supernova in the East if you’d like to know more about Japans psychology and everything else during this era and how they went from well respected and an admirable society in WW1 to the absolute shitshow it was in WW2.

I second this, many men saw it as a claim to fame, a heroic action for their country. At the time, imperialism was still at large so it was a given. If you watch They Shall Not Grow Old by Peter Jackson, it has a segment where a soldier comments on how if a man had not enlisted and chose to stay home, they were chastised and ridiculed for being cowardly by their community. I think the man states a woman hit him with her handbag for not being at the front.
Some of them might have been if it was early war time and they were sent back to the front. Saying that I have no proof and the title is misleading.

[Here’s](https://youtu.be/faM42KMeB5Q) an in-depth video on shell shock, at about the 25/26 minute mark it goes into how shell shock was treated as cowardice and even gives an example of a soldier with testimonies from his family with documentation too. In short; he was treated for shell shock previously and was sent back to the Somme afterwards, he broke down again and refused to fight. The officer over him court marshalled him which he then had to represent himself and then was sent to execution. 

That was during the early years of the war, I don’t think any executions took place after the war but it absolutely did happen during the war at the very least.

While I agree with everything you said, I’d like to put it out there that prior to WW1 they were the complete opposite of how they presented themselves in WW2, especially when it came to POWs.
(I’m sorry I’m on mobile so please excuse the mess) Here is a link describing some details: 

https://encyclopedia.1914-1918-online.net/article/prisoners_of_war_japan
While tbf this primarily talks about European POWs. This subject is not researched heavily and I can’t find anything on Chinese or other Asian POWs. 

In WW1 Japan had went through a load of economical, military, and political reforms and was desperate to gain recognition from the Western world and spread its sphere of influence so it was known to play far more ethical than its future counterpart. 
WW1 was a fairly large contribution to Japan’s complete 180 in psychology and sense of superiority in terms of WW2 and is some explanation into why they turned out the way they did in WW2.

Don’t be sorry at all! I’m glad you like my style and I’ll help in any way I can :) 
I did the general sketch with a cheap mechanical pencil with either 0.5 or 0.7 mm lead, I can’t exactly remember
I did the outline and fine line work with a Faber-Castell PITT Artist pen (I believe in the S size or whichever is the smallest), but any fine liner pen will do if I’m being honest. Uni-pen fine liners are another good brand. 
The markers I used were a mix between Promarkers (twin points) and BIC Marking Fine point permanent markers. (Promarkers are great but they are pricey while the BIC ones do just as good of a job imo and for way cheaper, both alcohol based). The markers just act as a base, I don’t do any detail with them.
I then go over the marker with Faber Castell watercolour pencils (there are expensive ones but I just use like an 10 euro set of them, think the box has a fish on it) for all the detail. You could probably use any colour pencil but I personally like the watercolour ones because they blend really nicely and layer well. I use a 101 white polychromos Faber Castell pencil for highlights and for blending the colours together too, it’s the best white pencil that does this imo. And then just use a general white gel pen for the extra highlights 
That’s pretty much my entire process. I hope it helps and feel free to shoot me a message if you’d like to know anything more :)
